body:
Purpose and Introduction

The Agnipath Scheme is a recruitment arrangement for personnel below officer rank in the Indian Army, Indian Navy and Indian Air Force. The Union Cabinet approved the scheme on 14 June 2022. Personnel recruited under it are known as Agniveers.

The original policy sought to introduce a younger personnel profile and provide opportunities for military service, training and skill development. It differs from traditional long-term military recruitment because it initially envisaged a fixed period of service followed by selective entry into the regular cadre.

Agnipath does not recruit personnel into the BSF, CISF or Indian Coast Guard. Those organizations have their own recruitment frameworks.

The Original 2022 Model

Under the scheme announced in 2022:

  • Agniveers were enrolled under the applicable service laws for an initial period of 4 years.
  • The standard entry-age range was 17.5 to 21 years, subject to recruitment rules and announced exceptions.
  • Selection, medical eligibility, education and service requirements depended on the relevant recruitment category.
  • Up to 25% of a batch could be selected for regular enrolment after completing the initial engagement, based on service requirements and objective criteria, including performance during the 4-year engagement.
  • Personnel completing their short engagement without regular enrolment were to receive the applicable Seva Nidhi package rather than a regular military pension for the short engagement alone.

There was a one-time upper-age relaxation to 23 years for the 2022 recruitment cycle. That exception should not be mistaken for the original standard age limit applicable to all later recruitment cycles.

Cabinet Decision of 4 November 2026

On 4 November 2026, the Ministry of Defence announced an important change following the Cabinet’s assessment of the scheme’s first 4 years.

The government retained the provision under which 25% of Agniveers could receive regular employment on merit, as envisaged earlier. It also approved an additional engagement period of 2 years for willing personnel among the remaining 75%.

After completing that additional period, these personnel would be offered enrolment as regular soldiers subject to their willingness and meeting the applicable selection criteria. The announcement also provided for higher remuneration, an enhanced Seva Nidhi package and seniority benefits during the additional engagement.

What the change does not mean

The decision must not be simplified into an unconditional statement that every Agniveer automatically becomes a permanent soldier after 4 or 6 years. The official announcement preserves conditions concerning willingness and selection. Detailed applicability to particular recruitment batches must be read with the relevant implementing instructions.

Understanding the 2 Pathways

The original and revised arrangements can be understood by separating regular enrolment at the end of the initial 4-year period from the newly approved additional 2-year engagement for other willing Agniveers.

These categories represent policy pathways rather than a guarantee that every individual will choose or qualify for the same outcome. The government’s 4 November 2026 announcement is the relevant current policy statement for this lesson’s 16 November 2026 cutoff.

Why the Distinction Matters for Prelims

A question may refer to the initial 2022 model or to the November 2026 decision. The correct answer depends on the date of the statement being tested.

For example, the description that Agnipath was introduced in 2022 with an initial 4-year engagement is a historical fact. The assertion that the remaining 75% have no possibility of further engagement is no longer an adequate description of the policy after the November 2026 announcement.

Prelims focus

  • Agnipath approved: 14 June 2022.
  • Recruited personnel are called Agniveers.
  • Initial engagement under the original scheme: 4 years.
  • Original merit-based regular-enrolment provision: up to 25%.
  • Cabinet announcement on 4 November 2026: additional 2-year engagement for willing personnel among the remaining 75%.
  • Trap: The additional engagement and subsequent regular enrolment involve stated conditions; they must not be described as unconditional automatic appointments.

[Sources: Ministry of Defence, Cabinet Clears Agnipath Scheme for Recruitment of Youth in the Armed Forces, 14 June 2022, PIB release 1833747, sections on terms, age and regular enrolment; Ministry of Defence, Extension of Entry Age: Agnipath Scheme, 17 June 2022, PIB release 1834658; Ministry of Defence, Cabinet Creates a Pathway for All Agniveers to Be Absorbed in Defence Forces, 4 November 2026, PIB release 2332524. Original-policy date: 14 June 2022; revised-policy announcement: 4 November 2026; content cutoff: 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: After 4 years, up to 25% may enter regular service on merit; the 2026 route gives willing others 2 more years, followed by conditional selection.
pictures.caption: The 2026 decision added a conditional further-service pathway after the initial 4 years.

title: Agnipath Recruitment: Original Scheme and the November 2026 Reform

body:
Understanding a Military Operation

An operation is an organized activity undertaken to achieve a defined objective. In defence current affairs, an operation may involve national security, evacuation, disaster relief, medical assistance or other authorized tasks.

It is important not to assume that every named operation is a combat operation. The Indian armed forces also conduct humanitarian missions and assist in evacuating people from emergencies abroad.

Operation Sindoor: May 2025

India launched Operation Sindoor on 7 May 2025, following the terrorist attack at Pahalgam on 22 April 2025, in which 26 civilians were killed.

The Indian government described the operation as a response directed against terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir. Its official statement on 7 May said that 9 sites had been targeted and that Pakistani military facilities were not among the targets selected for the initial action.

The stated objective was to act against infrastructure associated with cross-border terrorism. Subsequent Indian government releases described the operation as demonstrating coordinated action by the armed forces.

Figures describing targets and results in a conflict should be understood with their attribution. The figure of 9 targeted sites is from the Indian government’s official statement dated 7 May 2025; it should not be presented as an independently verified account of every subsequent military consequence.

Humanitarian and Evacuation Operations

India also uses military transport, naval vessels and medical capabilities to assist people affected by earthquakes, cyclones and armed conflict. These missions illustrate Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) and evacuation responsibilities.

OperationTime and placePurposeReported result or activity
Operation KaveriApril 2023; SudanEvacuate people during armed conflict.Indian Navy and Air Force assets supported the evacuation of Indian nationals.
Operation BrahmaMarch–April 2025; MyanmarAssist after the 28 March earthquake.Indian forces supplied relief, medical assistance and rescue support.
Operation SindoorMay 2025; Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and KashmirRespond to cross-border terrorism.India officially reported targeting 9 terrorist-infrastructure sites on 7 May 2025.
Operation Sagar Bandhu2025; Sri LankaAssist after Cyclone Ditwah.Indian agencies delivered relief supplies and supported evacuations and restoration work.

Operation Brahma: Disaster Relief in Myanmar

A major earthquake struck Myanmar on 28 March 2025. India responded through Operation Brahma, providing humanitarian supplies, medical teams and search-and-rescue assistance.

Indian government reporting published in February 2026 recorded approximately 750 tonnes of humanitarian assistance delivered and more than 2,500 patients treated by an Indian Army field hospital. These are reported results for the 2025 relief operation, not figures for a continuing programme in November 2026.

Operation Sagar Bandhu: Cyclone Relief in Sri Lanka

Operation Sagar Bandhu was undertaken after Cyclone Ditwah in 2025 to support Sri Lanka. The Indian response involved relief supplies, evacuation support and assistance with recovery.

A Government of India review released in February 2026 reported delivery of approximately 1,058 tonnes of relief material and evacuation of more than 2,500 people. These figures refer to the operation as reported by that review.

The operation should not be confused with Sagar Kavach, which is a coastal-security exercise, or with the broader policy vocabulary associated with India’s maritime cooperation.

How to Classify Operations Correctly

When reading a question about an operation, identify its date, location, objective and participating institutions. These facts often distinguish similarly named activities.

  • Security response: Operation Sindoor.
  • Conflict-zone evacuation: Operation Kaveri.
  • Earthquake relief: Operation Brahma.
  • Cyclone relief: Operation Sagar Bandhu.

A military operation can involve several services without being an exercise. Conversely, an exercise can rehearse a disaster-response scenario without being a real disaster-relief mission.

Prelims focus

  • Operation Sindoor began on 7 May 2025 after the Pahalgam terrorist attack of 22 April 2025.
  • India officially reported 9 targeted sites in its initial Operation Sindoor statement.
  • Operation Kaveri: evacuation from Sudan in 2023.
  • Operation Brahma: earthquake relief in Myanmar in 2025.
  • Operation Sagar Bandhu: relief assistance to Sri Lanka after Cyclone Ditwah in 2025.
  • Trap: Operation Sagar Bandhu and Exercise Sagar Kavach are different activities.

[Sources: Ministry of Defence, Operation Sindoor: Indian Armed Forces Carried Out Precision Strike at Terrorist Camps, 7 May 2025, PIB release 2127370; Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Operation Sindoor: Forging One Force, 18 May 2025, PIB release 2129453; Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Beyond Battlefield: Indian Armed Forces in Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief, 15 February 2026, PIB release 2228319, sections on Operations Kaveri, Brahma and Sagar Bandhu. Event periods: 2023 and 2025; reported-result status: February 2026; consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Operation Brahma illustrates the humanitarian role of India’s armed forces after a natural disaster.

title: Recent Indian Defence Operations: Purpose, Events and Outcomes

body:
Purpose of Defence Exercises

A defence exercise is a planned training and assessment activity. Forces use exercises to improve coordination, preparedness, communication and their ability to work with other organizations or partner countries.

An exercise differs from an operation conducted in response to an actual incident. Exercises may include simulated situations and practical training, but their main purpose is preparation and assessment rather than reporting the result of a real conflict.

For prelims, the most useful identifying details are the exercise name, participating forces or countries, location, date and primary purpose.

Exercises with Direct Gujarat Relevance

Trishul 2025

Tri-Services Exercise Trishul was conducted in November 2025 with the Indian Navy as the lead service. The Indian Army and Indian Air Force participated, along with the Indian Coast Guard, BSF and other agencies.

It covered the creek and desert sectors of Gujarat and Rajasthan and maritime areas of the northern Arabian Sea. The exercise was conducted from 3 to 13 November 2025, with a concluding activity on the Gujarat coast.

According to the Ministry of Defence’s report dated 14 November 2025, its principal purpose was to improve inter-service coordination and validate integrated procedures. The reported outcome was the completion of the planned tri-service exercise and assessment of joint preparedness.

For a Gujarat-focused question, the combination of Trishul, November 2025, Gujarat, Rajasthan, northern Arabian Sea and tri-service participation is the key identification set.

Sagar Kavach

Sagar Kavach is a coastal-security exercise involving the Indian Coast Guard, Navy, Marine Police and other relevant agencies. It tests coordination among institutions responsible for coastal security.

Its focus is narrower than that of a large tri-services military exercise. It is concerned particularly with preparedness against threats from the sea and with the effectiveness of coastal-security arrangements.

Major Naval Exercises

TROPEX

TROPEX stands for Theatre Level Operational Readiness Exercise. It is a major Indian Navy exercise intended to assess maritime readiness and coordination.

TROPEX-25 was conducted during January–March 2025. The Indian Navy participated alongside elements from the Indian Army, Air Force and Coast Guard. The Ministry of Defence described the exercise as an assessment of the Navy’s preparedness and ability to protect maritime interests through coordinated responses.

The word theatre in TROPEX is part of the name of an exercise. It does not mean that a proposed integrated theatre command had been established.

Malabar

Exercise Malabar is a multinational naval exercise involving the navies of India, the United States, Japan and Australia. It promotes maritime cooperation and interoperability.

Its 2025 edition was held around Guam. The participating countries are an especially useful distinguishing fact because Malabar is sometimes confused with bilateral naval exercises.

Varuna

Exercise Varuna is a bilateral naval exercise between India and France. Its 2025 edition was conducted from 19 to 22 March 2025. It is associated with naval cooperation and improving interoperability between the 2 navies.

Army, Air Force and Humanitarian Exercises

Yudh Abhyas

Yudh Abhyas is a bilateral India–United States Army exercise. The 2025 edition was conducted in Alaska from 1 to 14 September 2025. It develops cooperation and mutual understanding between the participating armies, including relevant peacekeeping and joint-training activities.

Tarang Shakti 2026

Exercise Tarang Shakti 2026 was a major Indian Air Force-hosted multinational air exercise at Air Force Station Jodhpur, Rajasthan, from 26 September to 12 October 2026.

The Ministry of Defence stated on 12 October 2026 that the exercise brought together participating air forces from 7 foreign countries: Australia, Bangladesh, France, Germany, Sri Lanka, the United Arab Emirates and the United States. It also involved 32 observer nations.

This was the second edition, following the inaugural edition in 2024. Its purpose was to promote cooperation and interoperability among participating air forces. The concluding government release described the exercise as successfully providing a platform for joint training and the exchange of experience.

Tiger Triumph

Tiger Triumph is an India–United States tri-service exercise emphasizing Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief. Its 2025 edition took place from 1 to 15 April 2025 in the Visakhapatnam–Kakinada region.

The important distinction is that Tiger Triumph rehearses cooperation for humanitarian scenarios, while Operation Brahma was an actual relief response to the Myanmar earthquake.

One-Glance Comparison

ExerciseMain participantsIdentification fact

Tiger Triumph 2025India and United StatesTri-service humanitarian-assistance exercise.

Connecting Gujarat Security with National Defence

The full subject can be understood as 3 connected areas. First, geography explains why Gujarat’s Arabian Sea coastline, Kutch and Sir Creek require particular attention. Second, institutions explain how the Navy, Coast Guard, Marine Police and BSF perform different but related roles. Third, reforms and current affairs explain how the CDS, theatre-command proposals, Agnipath, operations and exercises fit into India’s defence framework.

These categories should remain distinct. Sir Creek is a border dispute; the Coast Guard is an institution; the Coastal Security Scheme is a government initiative; Agnipath is a recruitment scheme; Trishul is an exercise; and Sindoor is an operation.

Prelims focus

  • Trishul 2025: tri-services exercise involving Gujarat, Rajasthan and the northern Arabian Sea.
  • Malabar: India, United States, Japan and Australia.
  • Varuna: India–France naval exercise; Yudh Abhyas: India–United States Army exercise.
  • TROPEX: Theatre Level Operational Readiness Exercise of the Indian Navy.
  • Tarang Shakti 2026: Indian Air Force-hosted exercise at Jodhpur, 26 September–12 October 2026, with 7 participating foreign countries and 32 observer nations.
  • Trap: An exercise, an actual operation, a security institution and a defence-reform proposal are not interchangeable.

[Sources: Ministry of Defence, Culmination of Tri-Services Exercise 2025: Trishul, 14 November 2025, PIB release 2189935; Ministry of Defence, 2025 defence-service reviews, PIB release 2210154, sections on TROPEX, Trishul and Tiger Triumph; Ministry of Defence, Varuna 2025 exercise release, 24 March 2025; Ministry of Defence, Yudh Abhyas 2025 exercise announcement, September 2025; Ministry of Defence, Malabar 2025 naval exercise announcement, November 2025; Ministry of Defence, Exercise Tarang Shakti 2026: Power in Partnership, Strength in Self-Reliance, 12 October 2026, PIB release 2322365; Ministry of Home Affairs, Training of Coastal Police, 17 December 2024, PIB release 2085166. Exercise facts reflect the specified 2025 and 2026 editions; consulted 16 November 2026.]
